about.title: Costa Mesa Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Costa Mesa is built around places people walk through every day: the retail strips and parking structures along Harbor Boulevard, the restaurants and shops lining Newport Boulevard, apartment complexes, gyms, grocery stores, and office lobbies. When a floor is wet with no sign posted, a stairway light has been out for weeks, or a parking-lot pothole goes unpatched, the person who falls often ends up carrying the cost alone. California premises liability law says that shouldn't be automatic. If a property owner or business knew about a hazard, or reasonably should have discovered it, and did nothing to fix it or warn visitors, they can be held responsible for the harm. That word, notice, is where many Orange County fall claims are won or lost, which is why what you do in the first few days matters so much. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect people injured in Costa Mesa with an independent attorney who handles premises cases on contingency, so you owe nothing unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Costa Mesa Residents Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Notice has to be proven, not assumed
items.desc: California requires the injured person to show the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney in our network knows how to dig for inspection logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that establish that knowledge.

items.title: Video disappears fast
items.desc: Most Harbor Boulevard and Newport Boulevard businesses run surveillance cameras, but footage is routinely overwritten within days or weeks. Getting a preservation letter out early can be the difference between a clear record and a he-said-she-said dispute.

items.title: The clock runs differently depending on who owns the property
items.desc: You generally have two years to file against a private owner in California, but a fall on city, county, or state property triggers a much shorter government claim deadline. A connected attorney can sort out ownership before a deadline quietly passes.

items.question: I fell on a cracked sidewalk or in a public park in Costa Mesa. Is my deadline still two years?
items.answer: Probably not. When the property belongs to a public entity such as the City of Costa Mesa, Orange County, or the State of California, you typically must file a formal government claim within six months of the injury before a lawsuit is even allowed. Figuring out who actually owns or maintains the spot where you fell is one of the first things an attorney will do, and it's a reason not to wait.

items.question: The store manager said I should have been watching where I was going. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: No. California uses pure comparative fault, which means your recovery can be reduced by whatever share of blame is assigned to you, but it isn't wiped out. If a spill sat on the floor for an hour with no cone or sign, the owner's failure to warn still counts heavily, even if you were looking at your phone. An attorney can push back on attempts to shift all the responsibility onto you.

items.question: What should I do right after a fall if I'm able?
items.answer: Photograph the hazard and the surrounding area before it gets cleaned or repaired, and note the time. Ask for an incident report and the names of any witnesses or employees who saw what happened. Get medical care even if you think it's just a bruise, since fall injuries often show up later. Then reach out, and LawProactive will connect you with an independent attorney who can request surveillance footage before it's erased.
